name: דיפרנציאל של f:R²→R² וקירוב לינארי בנקודה סמוכה (באנגלית)
questiontext:
Let \( f:R^2 \rightarrow R^2 \) defined as:

\[f(x,y)=({{CT:0}} , {{CT:1}})\]

a

Calculate the differential of \(f(x,y)\):

\(Df(x,y)=\) [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
b

Calculate the linear approximation for the function in a nearby point for each coordinate:

\[f({{CT:2}}+\frac{{{CT:3}}}{100},{{CT:4}}+\frac{{{CT:5}}}{100})\]

[[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]

Enter the approximation as a list of its two coordinates, for example [a,b].
generalfeedback:
Outline: Differentiate each coordinate function with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) to get the Jacobian matrix, evaluate \(f\) and the Jacobian at the base point \(({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})\), and use \(f(p_0+h)\approx f(p_0)+Df(p_0)\,h\).
Step 1 — The differential (part a)
The differential of \(f=(f_1,f_2)\) is the \(2\times 2\) Jacobian matrix: row \(i\) holds the partial derivatives of \(f_i\) with respect to \(x\) and \(y\).

\[ \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}={{CT:6}},\qquad \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}={{CT:7}} \]

\[ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}={{CT:8}},\qquad \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}={{CT:9}} \]

Hence

\[ Df(x,y)={{CT:10}} \]

Step 2 — Values at the base point
The nearby point is \(({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})+\left(\frac{ {{CT:3}} }{100},\frac{ {{CT:5}} }{100}\right)\), so we linearize at \(({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})\):

\[ f({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})=\left({{CT:11}},\ {{CT:12}}\right),\qquad Df({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})={{CT:13}} \]

Step 3 — The linear approximation (part b)
\(f(p_0+h)\approx f(p_0)+Df(p_0)\,h\) with \(h=\left(\frac{ {{CT:3}} }{100},\frac{ {{CT:5}} }{100}\right)\), coordinate by coordinate:

\[ f_1\approx {{CT:11}}+\left({{CT:14}}\right)\cdot\frac{ {{CT:3}} }{100}+\left({{CT:15}}\right)\cdot\frac{ {{CT:5}} }{100}={{CT:16}} \]

\[ f_2\approx {{CT:12}}+\left({{CT:17}}\right)\cdot\frac{ {{CT:3}} }{100}+\left({{CT:18}}\right)\cdot\frac{ {{CT:5}} }{100}={{CT:19}} \]

So

\[ f\left({{CT:2}}+\frac{ {{CT:3}} }{100},{{CT:4}}+\frac{ {{CT:5}} }{100}\right)\approx {{CT:20}} \]

(entered as a list of the two coordinates).

prts.name: prt1

on_false.feedback:
Part a — incorrect. Not all of the partial derivatives are correct.
\( \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}(x,y) {@feed[1]@} \)
\( \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}(x,y) {@feed[2]@} \)
\( \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}(x,y) {@feed[3]@} \)
\( \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}(x,y) {@feed[4]@} \)

on_true.feedback: Well Done! The differential \( Df(x,y) \) is correct.

on_false.feedback:
The answer is partially correct!

All The partial derivatives are correct, but not on the right order in the matrix.

The right answer is \({{CT:10}}\)
The approximation is not in the right format.

on_true.feedback:
Part b — correct. The Approximation is correct.

The difference, by coordinates, between your estimate and the actual value of \(f({{CT:2}}+\frac{{{CT:3}}}{100},{{CT:4}}+\frac{{{CT:5}}}{100})\) is {@differ@}

on_false.feedback:
The approximation is incorrect.

We can approximate the value of the function \(f(x,y)\) around the point \(({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})\).

\( f(x,y)=f({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})+\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}}) & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})\\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})& \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}}) \end{bmatrix} \cdot \left( \begin{bmatrix}x\\ y \end{bmatrix}- \begin{bmatrix} {{CT:2}}\\{{CT:4}} \end{bmatrix} \right) \)

Therefore,

\( f({{CT:2}}+\frac{{{CT:3}}}{100},{{CT:4}}+\frac{{{CT:5}}}{100})=f({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})+\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}}) & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})\\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}})& \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}({{CT:2}},{{CT:4}}) \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \frac{{{CT:3}}}{100}\\\frac{{{CT:5}}}{100} \end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix} {{CT:16}}\\{{CT:19}} \end{bmatrix} \)
